title: Upekkha as a subject
hookLine: a mother with four sons, and the one busy with his own life: how equanimity loves
tomorrow: what's left when the object is gone and only space remains?

lines: THE LAST BOX TO THE CAR.
THE ONE WITH HIS OWN LIFE.
cards: Moving-out day. A parent carries the last box to the car, hugs too long, and then stands in the driveway with empty hands. The Visuddhimagga has a picture for that driveway.
A mother has four sons. The little one, she wants to see grow. The sick one, she wants well.
The one in the bloom of youth, she wants to keep his good fortune. And the grown one, busy with his own affairs: about him, she isn't anxious. She still loves him.
She lets his life be his.

teach.b: Those four sons are the four boundless states: kindness, compassion, gladness, and upekkha, equanimity. Equanimity isn't the son loved least. It's love for someone who has to walk his own road.
As a meditation subject the manual starts with a neutral person, and the reflection is old and plain: beings are owners of their kamma, their actions.
Their happiness and their pain come along their own road, not only by my wishing. That's why equanimity comes fourth. It doesn't replace the other three; it rests on them.

The manual also names a counterfeit, the near enemy: a blank indifference that doesn't know or care, which can look calm from outside. And two far enemies, greed and resentment, the grab and the shove.
Equanimity sits between them like a level on a shelf: not tipped toward clutching, not tipped toward pushing away.

how: Equanimity is the fourth of the four boundless states, the brahmaviharas; in the Visuddhimagga's method it begins with a neutral person and is developed after kindness, compassion and gladness.

games.q: what does “upekkha as a subject” mean?
o: not caring at all how things turn out
a level, caring calm that lets lives be their own
keeping your feelings hidden from everyone

games.q: the four sons — tap the pairs.
p: the son in the bloom of youth
gladness: may his good fortune last
the son busy with his own life

s: equanimity means not caring how things turn out
that blank indifference is its near enemy; equanimity rests on kindness, compassion and gladness.
in the manual's picture, equanimity is the mother's love for her grown son busy with his own affairs
not loved less: loved as someone walking his own road.

games.q: your best friend is choosing a college you think is a mistake. you've already said your piece, twice. what does upekkha look like now?
o: keep pushing until she sees it your way; that's what caring is.
tell her you don't care where she goes; it's her problem.
keep caring, and let the choice be hers: her life, her road.
games.why: beings are owners of their actions, the manual says. equanimity doesn't stop caring; it stops pulling. the far enemies are the grab and the shove.

practice: Sit with both feet flat and rock gently left and right a few times, then settle where your weight is even. Hold someone you care about in mind from there, and on each out-breath let the thought rest: their life is theirs to live.

wordCard.voice: Upekkha as a subject: equanimity made the object of meditation. Caring fully, then letting each life be its own. The fourth boundless state.

orig.note: Pali: equanimity, looking on evenly; the Sanskrit is upeksha.

carryVoice: Keep this one: equanimity, a level heart that still cares. Thirty-two days into the forty.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 9 (equanimity: begin with a neutral person; beings are owners of their deeds; near enemy the equanimity of unknowing, far enemies greed and resentment; the simile of a mother with four sons for the four divine abidings)
